title: ROAD: Modern Adversarial Training for Simple One-Step Distillation at Scale

paper.title: ROAD: Modern Adversarial Training for Simple One-Step Distillation at Scale
paper.abstract:
Abstract One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators,
but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute.
Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at
modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded
One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills
text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight
representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional
head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head
with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed
random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to
generator–critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and
periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective.
Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input–logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1’s limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single
adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on
SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a
fraction of distribution matching’s training compute.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow models have achieved remarkable quality in text-to-image generation, but their iterative sampling remains expensive at inference time. Step distillation therefore aims to compress a many-step generator into one or a few evaluations. Paradoxically, however, the strongest one-step methods often simplify inference by making training substantially more complicated: distribution matching introduces an online score network at base-model scale [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , while competitive systems commonly rely on additional objectives, auxiliary models, or multiple stages (Tab. 2 , Sec. D ). Thus, one-step inference has become simple, but one-step training has not . Adversarial distillation offers a strikingly simpler alternative. Rather than matching scores or trajectories, it can train a one-step generator directly against real data with a single adversarial objective, without an online score network or repeated teacher queries. Yet this simplicity has not carried over to modern text-to-image models. Pure adversarial training at this scale has struggled with stability and prompt alignment [ 6 , 1 ] . As a result, adversarial losses are typically used only to assist a heavier distillation objective [ 6 , 7 ] . When adversarial training becomes the main objective, existing methods often recover performance by introducing other sources of complexity, such as teacher-generated supervision, previously distilled generators, or large trainable critics [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . This leaves open a more fundamental question: is pure adversarial distillation itself unable to scale, or is the critic used to train it the actual bottleneck? We investigate the latter possibility. The critic used in adversarial distillation is largely inherited from projected GANs [ 11 , 12 ] , while the representation space it operates on has changed substantially. Modern visual encoders such as DINOv3 and Perception Encoder already map images into contextual, semantically organized token representations [ 13 , 14 ] . Yet these representations are still read through lightweight convolutional heads; the random feature transform is sampled once and held fixed throughout training; and gradient regularization acts only on a scalar obtained by pooling the dense critic outputs. We find that these seemingly innocuous design choices become increasingly restrictive at modern model scale. They limit how the critic interprets semantic representations, allow its judgments to become increasingly tied to a single feature view during prolonged optimization, and leave individual logit sensitivities insufficiently controlled. This diagnosis leads us to revisit pure adversarial distillation with a modern critic tailored to today’s representations and optimization dynamics, making its simple training recipe effective at text-to-image scale. We instantiate this idea in ROAD, R epresentation-grounded O ne-step A dversarial D istillation. Reading modern representations with modern ViT heads. The inherited convolutional readout builds a visual pyramid over fixed neighborhoods, whereas modern token representations call for a head that selects and relates semantic evidence by content. We therefore use ViT heads made viable for adversarial training through Lipschitz controls, while cross-attention to individual prompt tokens improves text alignment. The resulting critic clearly outperforms similar-sized convolutional heads in fidelity and alignment (Sec. 3.1 ). Keeping the random mixing random. Projected critics read the frozen features through a random mixing, drawn once and held fixed so that the critic does not rely on a few dominant feature directions [ 11 ] . This protection, however, does not last over long horizons: training under a fixed draw converges quickly, then oscillates and slowly deteriorates. We attribute this to generator–critic co-adaptation around one persistent view of the representation: directions measured weakly by that view can remain poorly corrected. ROAD periodically redraws the mixing while carrying forward the generator, heads, and optimizer states. This changes the feature view without restarting learning, limits prolonged co-adaptation, and sustains improvement where fixed-mixing runs deteriorate (Sec. 3.2 ). Adapting R1 to dense, vector-valued critics. The classical R1 penalty regularizes a scalar critic through its input gradient on real images and is a staple of stable GAN training [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . ROAD’s critic, however, is dense and vector-valued, and the adversarial loss acts on every logit, whereas the customary extension pools the logits into a scalar before applying R1 [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Pooling keeps only one direction of the critic’s output space, so the input–logit Jacobian’s sensitivities in every other direction, however large, never enter the penalty. The proposed Jacobian R1 (JR1) instead penalizes every logit’s input gradient, i.e., the squared Frobenius norm of the input–logit Jacobian. A single unbiased Hutchinson probe makes it practical with one vector–Jacobian product (Sec. 3.3 ). ROAD proves to be a simple, low-cost, and strong one-step distillation method: with one loss and one stage, it reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K. On SDXL, it reaches the best FID of ODE-initialized DMD2 using 1/9.25 of the training GPU-hours (Fig. 1 ).

sections.heading: 3  Scaling Pure Adversarial Distillation with a Representation-Grounded Critic
sections.text: ROAD trains the one-step student with the dense adversarial losses and the JR1 penalty against a projected critic assembled from three parts: the frozen encoder, the random mixings, which ROAD periodically re-draws, and trainable Transformer heads that attend to the prompt’s text tokens and emit dense per-position logits (Fig. 2 ). The teacher appears only as the student’s initialization.

sections.heading: 3.1  A Transformer Head for Semantic Token Representations
sections.text: A natural starting point is to retain the convolutional discriminator design of Projected GAN [ 11 ] . In our one-step distillation setting, this convolutional (Conv) readout remains trainable but underperforms in both image quality and prompt adherence, and simply increasing its capacity (Deep Conv) further degrades performance, as shown in rows 1 and 2 of Tab. 1 , respectively. We attribute this to a change in what the trainable head is for. A modern ViT backbone such as DINOv3 already maps an image into a contextual, semantic representation space, and every tap returns the same number of tokens. The head need not rebuild the visual pyramid that projected GAN’s convolutional heads construct; it has only to decide which tokens matter and how they relate. Convolution aggregates over predetermined neighborhoods with fixed, translation-shared weights, an inductive bias suited to building a hierarchy from raw pixels rather than to reading backbone features: two tokens are combined because they are adjacent, not because their content is related. Self-attention decides instead from the tokens themselves which of them are combined and how strongly, which makes a Transformer head the more promising choice. This failure is consistent with a known difficulty: standard dot-product softmax attention is not globally Lipschitz in its inputs, even when the learned linear maps have bounded spectral norm [ 24 ] . A Lipschitz-controlled ViT head is therefore introduced, which constrains the gain of every trainable component through three complementary mechanisms. First, spectral normalization [ 23 ] is applied to every learned linear map in attention, the FFN, and the logit readout, so that its spectral norm is no more than 1. Second, cosine attention with a clamped temperature normalizes every query and key before their comparison under a learnable per-head temperature clamped at s max s_{\max} [ 25 ] . ( 7 ), proved as Lemma A.1 in Sec. A . With the controls in place, the ViT head trains successfully and substantially improves the quality of generated images (Tab. 1 , row 5 ). ViTGAN [ 26 ] provides an alternative ViT discriminator design, but remains inferior to our head under the same protocol (Tab. 1 , row 4 ). The weak prompt adherence long associated with adversarial distillation, however, persists [ 6 , 1 ] . Comparing text-conditioning schemes, we attribute this shortfall to the pooled prompt vector: a single pooled embedding cannot express fine-grained linguistic structure. Token-level text conditioning via cross-attention. The Transformer head admits token-level cross-attention naturally, and cross-attention provides a direct mechanism for image tokens at different spatial positions to interact differently with individual text tokens. We insert cosine cross-attention into the first block of every head, with subsequent blocks refining the conditioned representation through self-attention and FFN layer. Each level keeps its own text key/value projections, allowing different semantic depths to read the same prompt differently. Under the unified protocol, Miyato-style pooled-text projection provides only a minor improvement over the unconditional critic, whereas token-level cross-attention yields a much stronger gain in CLIP score (Tab. 1 , rows 6 - 8 ). Multi-branch random mixing. Projected GAN’s random mixing is tailored to a convolutional pyramid, where CCM is a 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution within a level and CSM adds 3 × 3 3{\times}3 convolutions between levels of differing resolution. A ViT backbone has no such pyramid, since all taps share one uniform patch-token grid, so both maps reduce to a plain 1 × 1 1{\times}1 convolution that mixes channels alone. We therefore replace each single-kernel mixing by an average of three size-preserving random convolutions over the patch tokens, with kernels 1 × 1 1{\times}1 , 3 × 3 3{\times}3 , and 5 × 5 5{\times}5 ; the summary token is transformed separately by a random linear map. The wider branches let a token’s mixed value draw on its spatial neighbors, so evidence is spread across positions as well as channels and depths. Sec. 4.3 shows the advantage of this design. These frozen multi-branch maps constitute the mixing M M that Sec. 3.2 re-draws, and Sec. B.1 gives its matrix form and analyzes its anisotropy.

sections.heading: 3.2  Periodic Mixing Refresh Prevents Critic Co-adaptation

With the Transformer head of Sec. 3.1 , training converges quickly to good performance, then begins to oscillate and slowly deteriorate (Fig. 3 a). The symptom resembles discriminator overfitting, yet standard augmentation remedies such as DiffAugment [ 27 ] and ADA [ 28 ] do not materially alleviate this late-stage degradation under fixed mixing (Sec. 4.3 ). We therefore examine other possible causes and finally focus on the random mixing, held fixed throughout training in the classical design. We argue that its anisotropy persistently biases long-horizon optimization toward the same feature directions. The generator and the critic then form a realization-specific co-adaptation around this single view, which eventually erodes generation quality. A persistent critic state. We diagnose the critic with two measurements, Pre-projection Feature Utilization Coverage (PFUC) and the logit margin (Sec. B.3 ). PFUC is the first-order sensitivity of the critic’s mean logit to each backbone channel before mixing, expressed in backbone coordinates. It settles after an early phase of training and barely moves thereafter (Fig. 3 b): the TV between consecutive profiles decays to a floor (Fig. 3 c). The logit margin is the batch-mean real logit minus the batch-mean generated logit, measuring how confidently the critic separates the two populations. After the first few thousand steps, the margin stays large and nearly stationary (Fig. 3 d), even though FID has already begun its usual oscillation and deterioration. Because the generator is still changing, a critic decision that has stopped moving is not by itself a healthy sign. sections.heading: 3.4  The complete recipe.
sections.text: So far, the three components accomplish modernization of projected GAN, addressing three degrees of freedom of a representation-space critic, what judges (Sec. 3.1 ), through what measurement (Sec. 3.2 ), and how sharply (Sec. 3.3 ). Together they make the minimal objective of Eq. ( 1 ) sufficient at modern text-to-image scale.

sections.heading: 4  Experiments
sections.text: Setup. We train one-step generators for SDXL [ 33 ] , a diffusion model with a UNet architecture, and SD3.5-M, a flow-matching model with an MMDiT architecture. Across the paper, DINOv3 ViT-B is chosen as the backbone for feature extraction unless otherwise specified. We use a dataset of 500K images from LAION-Aesthetic 5.5+ [ 34 ] built by DMD2. Following [ 1 , 6 , 35 ] , we evaluate on a random set of 10K COCO-2014 validation prompts. For both models we report FID, CLIP score, and aesthetic score. sections.heading: 5  Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: We modernize Projected GAN for one-step diffusion distillation with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head, a periodic refresh of the random mixing, and a Jacobian R1 penalty. The resulting method, ROAD, converges fast and attains the best FID on both SDXL and SD3.5-M with a single adversarial objective and one training stage, whereas competing methods combine several objectives and stages. To our knowledge, ROAD is among the first to obtain a competitive one-step SD3.5-M generator. Its preference scores, however, still trail those of few-step competitors (Tab. 3 ). Text reaches the critic only through cross-attention, so an explicit text–image alignment term is a natural next step, though it would mean replacing DINOv3 with a contrastively trained encoder such as SigLIP2 (Tab. 4.2 (b)). Scaling the frozen encoder does not help by itself either, since within DINOv3 ViT-B beats ViT-S and ViT-L (Tab. 4.2 (b)). We attribute this to the two-player game’s balance, which our refresh mechanism improves but does not settle, and addressing it directly is future work.

sections.heading: Appendix B Persistent Random Mixing: Analysis and Diagnostics
sections.text: This appendix supports Sec. 3.2 . We describe the implemented operator and its gain spectrum, make precise the sense in which a direction is weakly measured under a draw, and isolate the long-horizon consequence in a minimal measured-gap model. We report the empirical diagnostics in Sec. B.3 – B.4 and state the limits of the account in Sec. B.5 .

sections.heading: B.1  The implemented random mixing and anisotropy
sections.text: Random mixing in matrix form. Eq. ( 2 ) composes CCM and CSM along a top-down path, but it leaves the two operators unspecified. We specify them here, and, because the mixing path carries no nonlinearity, we follow each one through to the matrix that Sec. 3.2 reasons about. The construction proceeds in three steps: the matrix of one convolutional branch, then the matrix of one mixing, then the matrix through which the head of a given level reads. Setting. For both M ℓ cc M^{\mathrm{cc}}_{\ell} and M ℓ cs M^{\mathrm{cs}}_{\ell} , the patch tokens are reshaped to their two-dimensional grid. On a ViT backbone all L L taps share that grid, so every level carries the same number N p N_{\mathrm{p}} of patch positions, each of token width d d . The summary token is carried by its own random linear map, and it enters neither the matrices below nor the analysis that follows, so f ℓ f_{\ell} and f ^ ℓ \hat{f}_{\ell} denote the patch part of the level- ℓ \ell features throughout this appendix. We vectorize a level channel-major, so the features of one level form a vector of dimension N p ​ d N_{\mathrm{p}}d . Branch matrices. Each operator passes the grid through three independent, size-preserving d → d d\to d convolutions, whose 1 × 1 1{\times}1 , 3 × 3 3{\times}3 , and 5 × 5 5{\times}5 kernels are drawn by fan-in-scaled Kaiming-uniform initialization [ 48 ] . Write ℳ ⁡ ( W ) \mathcal{M}(W) for the matrix of one such convolution with kernel W W . A 1 × 1 1{\times}1 kernel W ( 1 ) ∈ ℝ d × d W^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} recombines channels and leaves positions untouched, so ℳ ⁡ ( W ( 1 ) ) = W ( 1 ) ⊗ I N p \mathcal{M}(W^{(1)})=W^{(1)}\otimes I_{N_{\mathrm{p}}} . A k × k k{\times}k kernel W ( k ) ∈ ℝ d × d × k × k W^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d\times k\times k} gives the standard matrix of a multi-channel two-dimensional convolution [ 49 , 50 ] . sections.heading: B.4  Longitudinal probes on a fixed-mixing run
sections.text: The fixed-run measurements in Sec. B.3 establish a persistent critic state, but they do not determine whether its separation is specific to the training realization M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} . We therefore apply two post-hoc diagnostics to frozen checkpoints of the same run. Fresh-draw transfer. At every 5 5 k-step checkpoint from 5 5 k to 30 30 k, we hold the checkpoint, critic head, and matched real and generated batches fixed, and replace only M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} by eight independently drawn mixings. The margin under M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} remains 5.1 5.1 – 5.3 5.3 through 25 25 k ( 4.5 4.5 at 30 30 k), whereas the margins under fresh draws are approximately zero at every checkpoint. Because only the mixing changes, this collapse shows that the fixed head’s real–generated separation does not transfer to a fresh measurement basis. This result directly supports its coupling to M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} . Linear probe. We also fit a separate linear classifier to the frozen mixed features at each level to distinguish real from generated samples. This classifier is used only as a diagnostic and does not update the generator, backbone, mixing, or critic. Beginning at approximately 2.5 2.5 k steps, real and generated samples are harder for a linear classifier to distinguish under M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} than under fresh draws, particularly for the shallow-level features. Over the same fixed-mixing run, FID oscillates and later worsens, whereas the margin under the fixed training mixing M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} remains large and nearly stationary. The fresh-draw and linear-probe diagnostics show that this separation is specific to the pairing D ϕ ∘ M ( 0 ) D_{\phi}\circ M^{(0)} .

sections.heading: B.5  Scope of the account
sections.text: The account makes two claims at different strengths. First, Prop. B.1 shows in a linear surrogate why weak-direction residuals persist under a fixed draw and why independent draws remove a permanently privileged direction in expectation. The chain-rule bounds of Sec. 3.2 tie the visibility and correction of a direction to its gain. Second, the realization-specific co-adaptation of Sec. 3.2 , in which prolonged optimization under the fixed gain landscape hardens both players around it until quality degrades, is a mechanistic reading of the ongoing nonlinear game. It is supported jointly by PFUC, the margin, the fresh-draw probes of Sec. B.4 , and the fixed-versus-refreshed intervention, but none of these alone establishes it.

sections.heading: Appendix D Related Work
sections.text: Few-step distillation of text-to-image diffusion models. Multi-objective or multi-stage training. The existing methods mostly use multiple training objectives and often consist of multiple training stages. Hyper-SD employs a six-phase hybrid training pipeline: four stages of trajectory-segmented consistency distillation, followed by human-feedback optimization and DMD-based one-step score distillation [ 39 ] . For the one-step SDXL model, DMD2 uses a two-stage pipeline consisting of brief regression pretraining followed by joint distribution-matching and adversarial training stabilized by a two-timescale update rule [ 1 , Sec. F.4] ; DMDX is also a two-stage pipeline, consisting of adversarial distillation pretraining on teacher-generated ODE pairs with hybrid latent- and pixel-space discriminators, along with adversarial distribution-matching fine-tuning [ 38 ] . SiDA jointly trains a one-step generator with score-identity and adversarial losses, reusing the fake score network’s encoder as a parameter-free discriminator [ 7 ] . ADD (SDXL-Turbo) uses single-stage joint training with teacher-based score distillation and a DINOv2-feature adversarial loss [ 6 ] . SDXL-Lightning employs a five-stage progressive distillation pipeline: one MSE-based trajectory-distillation stage followed by four adversarial stages [ 43 ] . NitroFusion uses dynamic adversarial refinement with a pool of conditional and unconditional global–local discriminators, relying on a DMD2 one-step student and four-step teacher [ 9 ] , so separate score-based pretraining is a prerequisite . SenseFlow combines score-based distribution matching, trajectory-based intra-segment guidance, and timestep-aware VFM adversarial supervision [ 44 ] . SwD produces a progressive few-step generator that increases latent resolution across denoising steps, combining patch-level MMD with score-based distribution matching and adversarial loss [ 42 ] . Adversarial objective as a single loss. Both APT [ 10 ] and LADD [ 8 ] perform latent-space adversarial training and derive multilevel discriminator features from pretrained diffusion models . LADD freezes the diffusion teacher, attaches discriminator heads to its intermediate features, and uses teacher-generated samples as real targets. APT initializes a separate discriminator from the pretrained diffusion model, adds multilevel output heads, and fine-tunes it against real data. D2O [ 18 ] converts a pretrained diffusion U-Net into a one-step generator through pure adversarial fine-tuning; it is evaluated only on low-resolution unconditional and class-conditional benchmarks and does not address text-to-image synthesis . Unlike APT and LADD, both of which use diffusion-based critics—trainable in APT and frozen in LADD—ROAD uses a frozen foundation model (e.g., DINOv3) with lightweight, prompt-conditioned Transformer heads. Compared with D2O, we propose Transformer heads, refreshed mixing, and JR1, thereby scaling pure adversarial training to large-scale text-to-image generation. Projected GAN and adjacent critic architectures. Convolutional heads over frozen encoders. Projected GAN trains shallow convolutional heads over a frozen pretrained encoder, whose features are scattered by fixed random cross-channel and cross-scale mixings [ 11 ] ; StyleGAN-XL scales it to ImageNet [ 55 ] , inheriting Projected GAN’s heads, and StyleGAN-T to text-to-image with 1-D convolutional heads over frozen ViT tokens [ 12 ] . Every head in this line is convolutional, the only reported head comparison being 1-D versus 2-D convolution [ 12 ] , and positions are scored independently, so the critic is vector-valued, a property ROAD keeps and regularizes. As far as we know, no work in this line attaches a Transformer head to frozen features. Transformer discriminators from scratch. ViTGAN scores a ViT on raw pixels from the class token, stabilized by L 2 L_{2} attention with tied query and key projections, and applies spectral normalization only to initialize the linear weights [ 26 ] . It reports that the vanilla ViT discriminator trains markedly worse than the stabilized one. TransGAN’s convolution-free discriminator ingests patches of several sizes [ 56 ] . Other work pairs Transformer generators with convolutional discriminators or embeds attention inside a CNN [ 57 , 58 , 59 , 60 ] . Our Lipschitz controls build on analyses of attention [ 24 , 61 ] , scaled cosine attention [ 25 ] , and spectral normalization [ 23 ] ; their combination into the projected critic’s ViT head with an explicit bound (Lemma A.1 ) and its conditioning on individual prompt tokens are new. Random feature mixing and time-varying discriminators. Fixed random mixing. Projected GAN samples the mixing once at initialization and holds it fixed for the whole run [ 11 ] , and every method in that line inherits the choice; the consequence of one draw persisting through long training, a critic that specializes to it, is, to our knowledge, unexamined. Previously, multiple-random-projection GANs train simultaneous discriminators on a fixed ensemble of input projections [ 62 ] , as do random-projection ensembles for classification [ 63 ] ; in both, the set of views is fixed in advance. Renewing trainable parameters. The closest precedents do alter the discriminator over time. NitroFusion keeps a pool of trainable heads, samples a subset per iteration, and re-initializes a small fraction of it, and SD3.5-Flash follows with stochastic head renewal [ 9 , 64 ] ; SDXL-Lightning resets its discriminator between progressive-distillation stages rather than within one [ 43 ] . Outside GANs, re-initializing trainable parameters is the standard remedy for lost plasticity, through last-layer resets, recycling of dormant neurons, shrink-and-perturb, and continual backpropagation [ 65 , 66 , 67 , 68 ] . Our ROAD instead re-draws the frozen measurement basis, the random mixings, at deterministic intervals while every trainable parameter persists, so it targets not lost plasticity in the head but the head’s specialization to a single persistent realization. Discriminator gradient regularization. Zero-centered penalties in GANs. Zero-centered discriminator-gradient penalties stabilize GAN training and admit local convergence analyses under suitable assumptions [ 69 , 15 ] , and R3GAN combines R1 and R2 [ 70 ] . D2O applies pooled R1 to the averaged logit [ 18 ] , ADD and P2D regularize in feature space [ 6 , 47 ] , and APT uses a finite-difference approximation [ 10 ] . Each constrains a scalar critic output, or an aggregate of a vector-valued one, which is the assumption our ROAD removes. Jacobian regularization in classification. Novak et al. [29] study the empirical relationship between input–output Jacobian sensitivity and generalization, whereas Jakubovitz and Giryes [71] explicitly regularize the logit Jacobian to improve adversarial robustness, and Varga et al. [30] , Hoffman et al. [32] develop efficient randomized Jacobian regularization. We apply a squared Jacobian-norm penalty to real images in a dense adversarial game, motivated specifically by the limitation of pooled R1, which aggregates the vector-valued logit (Sec. 3.3 ). Through Rademacher Hutchinson estimation [ 31 ] we recover the Jacobian energy in expectation with one input VJP per probe.

A block follows the pre-norm Transformer design. It contains a self-attention branch followed by an FFN branch, and the first block of every head contains a cross-attention branch between the two. sections.heading: E.2  Dataset and evaluation protocols
sections.text: Real-image training set. We use the fixed dataset of 500K real image–caption pairs constructed by DMD2 [ 1 ] from LAION-Aesthetics 5.5+ [ 34 ] for both SDXL and SD3.5-M. The dataset discards unsafe images and images whose width or height is below 1024 pixels. Model-specific decoding, resizing, and feature extraction are applied only after sampling from this common pool. COCO evaluation sets. For both models, we follow the DMD2 SDXL protocol without resampling its prompts or reference images. We use the fixed draw of 10K distinct images from the COCO-2014 validation set and one associated caption per image, as stored in the coco10k/all_prompts.pkl file and paired coco10k/subset directory . We generate one 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 image per prompt. The prompt order and sampling seeds are fixed and shared by all methods. FID and CLIP score. We compute FID with the DMD2 implementation of clean-fid in its clean mode. Before Inception feature extraction, the longer spatial dimension is center-cropped to form a square and the image is resized to 512 × 512 512\times 512 with Lanczos interpolation. The resulting FID compares 10K generated images with their corresponding 10K real images. We compute CLIP score with the DMD2 evaluator for both models. It center-crops each generated image, resizes it to 256 × 256 256\times 256 , and applies the OpenCLIP ViT-g/14 model pretrained on LAION-2B (laion2b_s12b_b42k). The text encoder receives the original caption prefixed by “A photo depicts”. We report the mean cosine similarity over all generated image–caption pairs. Auxiliary metrics. All auxiliary COCO metrics use the same generated images and the unmodified captions used by the corresponding FID evaluation. We report the mean raw score of LAION-Aesthetics Predictor V2, the official HPSv2 score [ 37 ] , and the score produced by yuvalkirstain/PickScore_v1 [ 36 ] . HPSv2 and PickScore are shown on the × 100 \times 100 scale used in the tables. ImageReward is the mean raw score from ImageReward-v1.0 [ 40 ] . GenEval [ 41 ] , reported only for SD3.5-M, is evaluated separately because it defines its own prompt suite. We use the released 553 prompts, generate four images per prompt, run the official Mask2Former/OpenCLIP evaluator with its default thresholds, and report the unweighted mean accuracy over its six compositional tasks. Checkpoint selection. We evaluate ROAD checkpoints every 500 training steps and select the checkpoint with the lowest FID. Every other metric in a row is computed from that same checkpoint; we never select a separate checkpoint for alignment, aesthetics, human preference, or GenEval. Public baselines are evaluated with the same prompt files, reference images, preprocessing, metric implementations, and reporting scales as the corresponding ROAD model.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.39539v1 [cs.CV] 29 Oct 2026 ROAD: Modern Adversarial Training for Simple One-Step Distillation at Scale Xiaoou Li Shan You Tao Huang Abstract One-step distillation turns pretrained diffusion models into fast generators, but strong results often require substantial training machinery and compute. Pure adversarial distillation offers a simpler route, yet has struggled at modern text-to-image scale. To address this limitation, we propose ROAD (Representation-grounded One-step Adversarial Distillation), a one-stage framework that distills text-to-image models with one adversarial objective and a lightweight representation-space critic. First, we replace the classical convolutional head with a Lipschitz-controlled Transformer head with token-level text conditioning, which matches the semantic tokens of modern visual encoders. Second, we observed a fixed random feature mixing leads to long-horizon degradation. We attribute it to generator–critic co-adaptation around one realization-specific view, and periodically re-draw the mixing to keep the randomization effective. Third, for our dense and vector-valued logits, we introduce Jacobian R1 which penalizes the full input–logit Jacobian, overcoming pooled R1’s limitation of neglecting most of logit sensitivities. A single adversarial objective then suffices: in one step, ROAD reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K, surpassing the multi-step teachers at a fraction of distribution matching’s training compute. Figure 1 : A single adversarial loss suffices for one-step distillation. Left: samples from ROAD. Right: one-step SDXL FID vs. training GPU-hours (our runs). DMD2 starts from the base model; DMD2-ODE init [ 1 , released recipe;] starts with a regression stage on teacher ODE pairs. ROAD needs no such stage, beats both baselines’ best FID early, and keeps improving. 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow models have achieved remarkable quality in text-to-image generation, but their iterative sampling remains expensive at inference time. Step distillation therefore aims to compress a many-step generator into one or a few evaluations. Paradoxically, however, the strongest one-step methods often simplify inference by making training substantially more complicated: distribution matching introduces an online score network at base-model scale [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , while competitive systems commonly rely on additional objectives, auxiliary models, or multiple stages (Tab. 2 , Sec. D ). Thus, one-step inference has become simple, but one-step training has not . Adversarial distillation offers a strikingly simpler alternative. Rather than matching scores or trajectories, it can train a one-step generator directly against real data with a single adversarial objective, without an online score network or repeated teacher queries. Yet this simplicity has not carried over to modern text-to-image models. Pure adversarial training at this scale has struggled with stability and prompt alignment [ 6 , 1 ] . As a result, adversarial losses are typically used only to assist a heavier distillation objective [ 6 , 7 ] . When adversarial training becomes the main objective, existing methods often recover performance by introducing other sources of complexity, such as teacher-generated supervision, previously distilled generators, or large trainable critics [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . This leaves open a more fundamental question: is pure adversarial distillation itself unable to scale, or is the critic used to train it the actual bottleneck? We investigate the latter possibility. The critic used in adversarial distillation is largely inherited from projected GANs [ 11 , 12 ] , while the representation space it operates on has changed substantially. Modern visual encoders such as DINOv3 and Perception Encoder already map images into contextual, semantically organized token representations [ 13 , 14 ] . Yet these representations are still read through lightweight convolutional heads; the random feature transform is sampled once and held fixed throughout training; and gradient regularization acts only on a scalar obtained by pooling the dense critic outputs. We find that these seemingly innocuous design choices become increasingly restrictive at modern model scale. They limit how the critic interprets semantic representations, allow its judgments to become increasingly tied to a single feature view during prolonged optimization, and leave individual logit sensitivities insufficiently controlled. This diagnosis leads us to revisit pure adversarial distillation with a modern critic tailored to today’s representations and optimization dynamics, making its simple training recipe effective at text-to-image scale. We instantiate this idea in ROAD, R epresentation-grounded O ne-step A dversarial D istillation. Reading modern representations with modern ViT heads. The inherited convolutional readout builds a visual pyramid over fixed neighborhoods, whereas modern token representations call for a head that selects and relates semantic evidence by content. We therefore use ViT heads made viable for adversarial training through Lipschitz controls, while cross-attention to individual prompt tokens improves text alignment. The resulting critic clearly outperforms similar-sized convolutional heads in fidelity and alignment (Sec. 3.1 ). Keeping the random mixing random. Projected critics read the frozen features through a random mixing, drawn once and held fixed so that the critic does not rely on a few dominant feature directions [ 11 ] . This protection, however, does not last over long horizons: training under a fixed draw converges quickly, then oscillates and slowly deteriorates. We attribute this to generator–critic co-adaptation around one persistent view of the representation: directions measured weakly by that view can remain poorly corrected. ROAD periodically redraws the mixing while carrying forward the generator, heads, and optimizer states. This changes the feature view without restarting learning, limits prolonged co-adaptation, and sustains improvement where fixed-mixing runs deteriorate (Sec. 3.2 ). Adapting R1 to dense, vector-valued critics. The classical R1 penalty regularizes a scalar critic through its input gradient on real images and is a staple of stable GAN training [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . ROAD’s critic, however, is dense and vector-valued, and the adversarial loss acts on every logit, whereas the customary extension pools the logits into a scalar before applying R1 [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Pooling keeps only one direction of the critic’s output space, so the input–logit Jacobian’s sensitivities in every other direction, however large, never enter the penalty. The proposed Jacobian R1 (JR1) instead penalizes every logit’s input gradient, i.e., the squared Frobenius norm of the input–logit Jacobian. A single unbiased Hutchinson probe makes it practical with one vector–Jacobian product (Sec. 3.3 ). ROAD proves to be a simple, low-cost, and strong one-step distillation method: with one loss and one stage, it reaches 11.03 FID on SDXL and 13.73 on SD3.5-M on COCO-10K. On SDXL, it reaches the best FID of ODE-initialized DMD2 using 1/9.25 of the training GPU-hours (Fig. 1 ). 2 Preliminaries Pure adversarial one-step distillation. The teacher appears only as the student’s initialization. 3.1 A Transformer Head for Semantic Token Representations A natural starting point is to retain the convolutional discriminator design of Projected GAN [ 11 ] . In our one-step distillation setting, this convolutional (Conv) readout remains trainable but underperforms in both image quality and prompt adherence, and simply increasing its capacity (Deep Conv) further degrades performance, as shown in rows 1 and 2 of Tab. 1 , respectively. We attribute this to a change in what the trainable head is for. A modern ViT backbone such as DINOv3 already maps an image into a contextual, semantic representation space, and every tap returns the same number of tokens. The head need not rebuild the visual pyramid that projected GAN’s convolutional heads construct; it has only to decide which tokens matter and how they relate. Convolution aggregates over predetermined neighborhoods with fixed, translation-shared weights, an inductive bias suited to building a hierarchy from raw pixels rather than to reading backbone features: two tokens are combined because they are adjacent, not because their content is related. Self-attention decides instead from the tokens themselves which of them are combined and how strongly, which makes a Transformer head the more promising choice. The Transformer head admits token-level cross-attention naturally, and cross-attention provides a direct mechanism for image tokens at different spatial positions to interact differently with individual text tokens. We insert cosine cross-attention into the first block of every head, with subsequent blocks refining the conditioned representation through self-attention and FFN layer. Each level keeps its own text key/value projections, allowing different semantic depths to read the same prompt differently.
